title: CloudPipe deployment inputs
description:
Every cluster-wide value a human supplies to stand up a CloudPipe deployment, and nothing else. `pixi run cloudpipe setup` reads this file rather than hard-coding its questions, and renders `terraform.tfvars` and `backend.tf` into a target Terraform root from the answers.

This is the integration contract for any front end. A caller reads it and renders a complete input form without opening another file: `title` is the prompt, `description` is the help text, `pattern` is the rule, `x-section` is the grouping, and `x-source` says where a human obtains the value. Fields marked `x-derived` are computed and overridable — a form generator must display the computed value and accept a change, but must NOT present them as questions.

The eight Globus variables are deliberately absent. `pixi run globus init` owns them and renders them into a separate `globus.auto.tfvars`; see `src/globus_admin/schemas/answers.schema.json`. The two sets are disjoint and a test holds them so, because two tools writing one variable is two tools disagreeing about it.

There is deliberately NO AWS credential, key, or profile field, and no Cloudflare API token field. AWS credentials come from the deployer's environment through an AWS CLI v2 SSO profile; the Cloudflare token comes from CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. Neither is ever prompted for, stored, or printed.

Every `pattern` here is the mechanical equivalent of a `validation` block in `terraform/modules/stack/variables.tf`, and `tests/test_setup_wizard_schema.py` derives both sides from that file and asserts they agree. A field whose variable Terraform does not constrain carries no pattern: one invented here would reject values Terraform accepts, which is the single failure a deployer cannot work around. `x-error-message` is Terraform's own `error_message`, verbatim, so the two can never word the same rule differently.

No value in this file identifies any deployment. Where a shape needs illustrating, the description uses a placeholder or a reserved example name.

x-required-when.state_bucket: The backend block is being rendered, which is the default. `cloudpipe setup --no-backend` skips both the file and this requirement.

region.x-error-message: region must be an AWS region id: two letters, a dash, a word, a dash, a digit.
region.title: AWS region
region.description: The region holding the cluster and almost everything else. Two things are always us-east-1 regardless of this value — ACM certificates attached to CloudFront, and the ECR Public token — which is why the example root configures that as a separate provider alias rather than deriving it.

uwmadison_prefix_list_id.x-error-message: uwmadison_prefix_list_id must be a prefix list ID (pl-...), not an ARN.
uwmadison_prefix_list_id.title: Institution ingress prefix list ID
uwmadison_prefix_list_id.description:
AWS managed prefix list of the IP ranges allowed to reach the web UIs over HTTPS: ArgoCD, Argo Workflows, Prefect, Kubecost and Grafana. An ID (pl-...), not an ARN. Create the prefix list in the VPC console with your institution's ranges first; this does not create it.

The variable name still says uwmadison. It is the reference deployment's name and means "the institution's ingress prefix list" here. Renaming it would need a Terraform `moved` block and a coordinated change across the example root and every tfvars file, so the wart is deliberate — you are not setting someone else's value.

domain.x-error-message: domain must be a bare DNS name with a TLD, e.g. example.org — no scheme and no trailing dot.
domain.title: Service domain
domain.description:
Where the services are published. Every service URL is derived from it. A Route53 hosted zone for this domain must already exist in the account you are deploying into — ACM validates its certificates against that zone, so a domain you do not own fails at apply rather than here. `cloudpipe preflight` checks for the zone before you get that far.

A bare DNS name: no scheme, no trailing dot.

institution_domain.x-error-message: institution_domain must be a bare email domain, e.g. example.edu.
institution_domain.title: Institution identity domain
institution_domain.description:
Who may sign in, which is a different question from where the services live and is frequently a different domain. The SSO proxies admit identities in this domain, and the ArgoCD admin address is built from it as <admin_netid>@<institution_domain>.

A bare email domain: no scheme, no @.

allOf.x-error-message: institution_oidc_issuer must be an https URL with no trailing slash.
institution_oidc_issuer must not end in a slash — the endpoint paths are appended to it.

institution_oidc_issuer.title: Institution OIDC issuer URL
institution_oidc_issuer.description:
Base URL of your institution's OIDC identity provider — the upstream Cloudflare Access and Dex authenticate against. The authorize, token and keyset endpoints are appended to it, so this must be the issuer the provider actually publishes at <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration. Cloudflare Access does not discover them.

An https URL with no trailing slash. `cloudpipe preflight` fetches the discovery document to confirm it is the right one. Your identity provider's administrator is the person who knows this value, and is usually the same person who registers the OIDC client for you.

admin_netid.title: Administrator username
admin_netid.description:
The one account allowed to enroll a WARP device and reach the cluster, and the account granted the ArgoCD admin role through Dex. A username only, not an address: the address is built as <admin_netid>@<institution_domain>.

No pattern is checked here, deliberately. A username convention belongs to your institution and the stack cannot know it, so a rule invented here would reject values that are correct. Terraform does not constrain it either.

github_repo.x-error-message: github_repo must be in owner/repo format, with no scheme and no .git suffix.
github_repo.title: CI repository (owner/repo)
github_repo.description:
The repository whose GitHub Actions runs may assume the ECR push and Packer AMI build roles. In owner/repo form: no scheme, no .git suffix.

Not necessarily the repository ArgoCD syncs — see gitops_repo_url. CI can run in one repository while the cluster follows another, and in the reference deployment it does.

gitops_repo_url.x-error-message: gitops_repo_url must be an https clone URL — ArgoCD reads it without a credential here.
gitops_repo_url.title: GitOps repository clone URL
gitops_repo_url.description:
The repository ArgoCD reads gitops/apps/ from, and that every generated Application tracks. An https clone URL: ArgoCD reads it without a credential, so an ssh URL does not work.

Deliberately separate from github_repo, which scopes the GitHub Actions trust policy. These may name the same repository or different ones.

github_user_url.x-error-message: github_user_url must be an https URL.
github_user_url.title: Repository owner URL
github_user_url.description: The owner's https URL — the organization or user page above your repositories. Used to scope the ArgoCD repository credential so that one credential covers every repository beneath it rather than one per repository.

github_oidc_allowed_subs.x-error-message: github_oidc_allowed_subs must not be empty: an empty list trusts nothing and every build loses its credentials.
github_oidc_allowed_subs.title: GitHub Actions OIDC subject claims
github_oidc_allowed_subs.description:
The exact `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` claim values allowed to assume the GitHub Actions roles. Derived from github_repo as main-branch runs only, which covers every workflow that assumes those roles today.

Override it when you need one of three things, all of which the stack's own variable documents: a non-main branch, temporarily, to test a build workflow before merging it; a job that sets a GitHub `environment:`, which mints repo:<repo>:environment:<name> and would NOT match a ref-shaped entry; or a wildcard, since the trust policy uses StringLike and `*` is a wildcard in these values.

An entry that matches nothing is not an error anywhere: the job simply loses its credentials. That is why this is derived rather than typed.

cloudflare_account_id.x-error-message: cloudflare_account_id must be the 32-character hex account id from the Cloudflare dashboard.
cloudflare_account_id.title: Cloudflare account ID
cloudflare_account_id.description: The account that owns the Zero Trust organization: 32 lowercase hex characters. It is in the Cloudflare dashboard URL once you have selected the account.

cloudflare_team_domain.title: Zero Trust team domain
cloudflare_team_domain.description: The Zero Trust team domain, <team>.cloudflareaccess.com. It is the organization's auth_domain and the host that WARP and the browser are sent to, so it has to match what Cloudflare assigned this account — it is not a name you choose here.

cloudflare_team_name.title: Zero Trust organization name
cloudflare_team_name.description:
The organization's name as Cloudflare generated it. A separate value from the team domain and NOT derivable from it: reading it back from the dashboard is the only way to get it right.

No pattern is checked here, deliberately — Cloudflare generates the value and there is no shape to check, which is also why Terraform does not constrain it. Get it wrong and nothing rejects it: the organization is silently renamed.

state_bucket.x-error-message: state_bucket must be a valid S3 bucket name.
state_bucket.title: Terraform state bucket
state_bucket.description:
The S3 bucket holding this deployment's Terraform state. It must exist before the first `terraform init`, and creating it is the one step the wizard will not take for you — nothing here creates an AWS resource. The closing output prints the commands that create it, enable versioning on it, and block public access to it.

Use a bucket dedicated to state, not the data bucket. Remote state is not optional in practice: local state is one laptop away from a deployment nobody can change, and versioning is what makes a truncated state recoverable. `cloudpipe setup --no-backend` skips the backend file entirely if you manage state another way.

state_key.title: Terraform state key
state_key.description: The object key the state is written to inside the bucket. The default is fine unless the bucket holds state for more than one deployment, in which case give each its own key — two roots sharing one key overwrite each other's state.

section.description: Field groupings, in the order a front end should present them. The identifiers are stable; the titles are display text.

source.description: Where a human obtains the value. A front end may group or annotate by this; the wizard shows it alongside the help text, because "go and look this up" is a different kind of answer from "decide this".
